title: B1 Writing Quiz 4 — Food, Health & Environment

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I ate less sugar, I would feel healthier.
If I eat less sugar, I would feel healthier.
If I ate less sugar, I will feel healthier.
If I would eat less sugar, I would feel healthier.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb: 'If I ate less sugar, I would feel healthier.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If they had recycled more, the town wouldn't produce so much waste.
If they had recycled more, the town wouldn't have produced so much waste.
If they recycled more, the town wouldn't have produced so much waste.
If they would have recycled more, the town wouldn't have produced so much waste.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If they had recycled..., the town wouldn't have produced...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This bread is baked fresh every morning.
This bread bakes fresh every morning.
This bread is baking fresh every morning.
This bread bake fresh every morning.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle: 'is baked fresh every morning.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The forest was damaged by the fire.
The forest damaged by the fire.
The forest was damage by the fire.
The forest is damaged by the fire.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: 'was damaged by the fire.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The doctor who treated me was very patient.
The doctor which treated me was very patient.
The doctor whom treated me was very patient.
The doctor, who treated me, was very patient but.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person: 'The doctor who treated me...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Organic farming, which is growing in popularity, helps protect the soil.
Organic farming which is growing in popularity helps protect the soil but.
Organic farming, that is growing in popularity, helps protect the soil.
Organic farming which is growing in popularity, helps protect the soil.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use commas and 'which' for things: 'Organic farming, which is growing in popularity, helps protect the soil.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: That can't be fresh fish, it smells odd.
That can't to be fresh fish, it smells odd.
That can't being fresh fish, it smells odd.
That cann't be fresh fish, it smells odd.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' + base verb expresses a confident negative deduction: 'that can't be fresh fish.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The recipe could be missing an ingredient.
The recipe could being missing an ingredient.
The recipe could to be missing an ingredient.
The recipe coulds be missing an ingredient.
questions.explanation: 'Could' + base verb expresses a possible deduction: 'the recipe could be missing an ingredient.'

questions.topic: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've tried three new recipes this week.
I've been trying three new recipes this week.
I've try three new recipes this week.
I'm trying three new recipes this week already.
questions.explanation: Present perfect simple is used for a completed number of results: 'I've tried three new recipes.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've been following a vegetarian diet for six months.
I've followed a vegetarian diet since six months.
I'm following a vegetarian diet for six months already.
I've been follow a vegetarian diet for six months.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an unfinished action: 'I've been following... for six months.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I have finished the diet plan.")
options: She said that she has finished the diet plan.
She said that she had finished the diet plan.
She said that she finished the diet plan already.
She said she have finished the diet plan.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect shifts back to past perfect: 'she had finished the diet plan.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "How often do you exercise?")
options: She asked me how often do I exercise.
She asked me how often I exercised.
She asked me how often did I exercise.
She asked me how often I exercise.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order (no auxiliary inversion) and shift the tense back: 'she asked me how often I exercised.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I used to eat fast food every day before I changed my habits.
I use to eat fast food every day before I changed my habits.
I was used to eat fast food every day before I changed my habits.
I used to eating fast food every day before I changed my habits.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'I used to eat fast food every day.'

questions.topic: Be used to / get used to
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'm used to cooking without meat now.
I'm used to cook without meat now.
I use to cooking without meat now.
I'm used cooking to without meat now.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund: 'I'm used to cooking without meat.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The doctor told him to cut down on salt.
The doctor told him to cut salt down on.
The doctor told him to cut down to on salt.
The doctor told him to cut on salt down.
questions.explanation: 'Cut down on' means 'reduce': 'cut down on salt.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She decided to give up smoking last year.
She decided to give smoking up to last year.
She decided to give up to smoking last year.
She decided to give smoking last year up.
questions.explanation: 'Give up' means 'stop doing something': 'give up smoking.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Despite the drought, the farmers had a good harvest.
Despite of the drought, the farmers had a good harvest.
Although the drought, the farmers had a good harvest.
Despite the drought was severe, the farmers had a good harvest.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (no 'of'): 'Despite the drought, the farmers had a good harvest.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Pollution levels rose sharply. As a result, the government banned old cars.
Pollution levels rose sharply, as a result the government banned old cars.
As a result pollution levels rose sharply the government banned old cars.
Pollution levels rose sharply as a result, the government banned old cars.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'Pollution levels rose sharply. As a result, the government banned old cars.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We don't have enough clean water in some regions.
We don't have water enough in some regions.
We don't have enough of water in some regions.
We hasn't enough water in some regions.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes before the noun it modifies: 'enough clean water.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Most people are aware of the dangers of plastic waste.
Most people are aware for the dangers of plastic waste.
Most people are aware to the dangers of plastic waste.
Most people are aware on the dangers of plastic waste.
questions.explanation: 'Aware of' + noun means 'conscious of': 'aware of the dangers.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to a nutritionist you haven't met, asking for advice?
options: Hey there,
Dear Dr. Ismayilova,
Yo,
Hiya,
questions.explanation: Using the recipient's title and name, 'Dear Dr. Ismayilova,' is a suitable formal opening.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email pitching an environmental project idea to a named contact?
options: Yours faithfully,
Kind regards,
Later,
Talk soon,
questions.explanation: 'Kind regards,' is a suitable semi-formal closing when writing to a named professional contact.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was wondering if you could suggest a healthier alternative.
I was wondering if you could to suggest a healthier alternative.
I was wondering could you suggesting a healthier alternative.
I wonder if you suggest could a healthier alternative.
questions.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could' + base verb is a polite way to make a request: 'if you could suggest an alternative.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the farmer.' and 'The farmer's vegetables won the prize.'?
options: This is the farmer whose vegetables won the prize.
This is the farmer who vegetables won the prize.
This is the farmer which vegetables won the prize.
This is the farmer's vegetables who won the prize.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: 'the farmer whose vegetables won the prize.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have never tried such a spicy dish before.
I have tried never such a spicy dish before.
Never I have tried such a spicy dish before.
I have tried such a spicy dish never before.
questions.explanation: 'Never' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle: 'I have never tried such a dish.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: I'd like to know whether the results have been confirmed.
I'd like to know whether have the results been confirmed?
I'd like to know, whether the results have been confirmed.
I'd like to know whether the results have been confirmed?
questions.explanation: Reported/indirect statements use normal word order and end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: This time tomorrow, I ___ a healthy breakfast for the whole family.
options: will cook
will be cooking
am cooking
cook
questions.explanation: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time: 'will be cooking'.

questions.question: By 2030, scientists ___ many new solutions for clean energy.
options: will develop
will have developed
develop
are developing
questions.explanation: Future perfect describes an action completed before a future point: 'will have developed'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses discourse markers.
options: Firstly, wash the vegetables. Secondly, chop them finely. Finally, add them to the pan.
Firstly we wash vegetables secondly chop finally pan.
Finally wash the vegetables, firstly chop, secondly add pan.
Secondly firstly wash vegetables, finally chop them.
questions.explanation: Discourse markers 'Firstly,', 'Secondly,' and 'Finally,' organize points clearly with commas.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You wouldn't waste food like that, would you?
You wouldn't waste food like that, do you?
You wouldn't waste food like that, wouldn't you?
You wouldn't waste food like that, will you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement with 'would' + positive tag: 'you wouldn't waste..., would you?'
